title: Canoe Place Chapel
summary: Canoe Place Chapel, built around 1819-1820, is a surviving place connected with Shinnecock Christian worship and community life at Canoe Place. Its history belongs to a wider landscape shaped by Shinnecock land, Rev. Paul Cuffee's ministry, nineteenth-century religious change, and later preservation.

why_this_matters: Canoe Place Chapel preserves a visible connection between Shinnecock community life and a place transformed by roads, rail, the canal, and land loss. The building also shows how Native Christian history can remain rooted in Indigenous kinship, land, and community authority.
history_content:
A 1797 Southampton map marks an "Indian Meeting House" east of the future Shinnecock Canal within land identified with the Shinnecock community. An 1829 map also marks a chapel in that area. These maps document Shinnecock worship at Canoe Place, but they do not by themselves prove that every marked building was the surviving chapel.

Canoe Place Chapel was built around 1819-1820 and served Native residents of the Canoe Place area. Rev. Paul Cuffee had preached at Canoe Place earlier as part of his regional ministry, connecting the chapel landscape with a longer Shinnecock and Unkechaug Christian history.

Later accounts describe an older meetinghouse being divided or moved during the nineteenth century, including a tradition associated with 1848. Surviving maps and local histories do not fully settle how the Canoe Place structure relates to the building moved to the Shinnecock Reservation, so that account remains qualified rather than presented as certain.

1
preservation_content:
Southampton Town acquired the chapel property through the Community Preservation Fund. The building was moved a short distance in 2015 and restoration continued through 2016 and 2017. The work protected the chapel as a public historic structure while keeping nearby ancestral and cemetery histories distinct from the building itself.
